title: Grammar Beyond the Sentence
orientation: Grammar connects ideas across sentences as well as inside them. In a report, research update or formal answer, readers must track participants, understand changing time reference and see why one claim follows another. This lesson develops those relationships through original short texts. It distinguishes cohesion, the visible links, from coherence, the meaningful organisation those links help readers recover. You will practise pronouns, substitution, ellipsis, topic progression, nominalisation and cautious academic claims. Earlier work on reference, voice, tense, information structure and modality will be revisited in paragraph contexts. The aim is to make each grammatical choice serve the message. A paragraph can contain legitimate tense and voice changes, and a concise version can still be inaccurate if it loses a qualification. Use the explanations and self-review rubrics to justify revisions rather than replacing every passive or repeated word automatically.
outcomes: Trace reference chains across several sentences.
Recover omitted grammatical material without creating fragments.
Explain purposeful changes of tense and voice.
Use transitions only for supported logical relations.
Revise compression and hedging without changing scope or certainty.

modules.title: Connecting sentences: cohesion, reference and recoverable omission
modules.definition: Cohesion consists of visible grammatical and lexical links across a text. Coherence is the interpretable connection among its ideas; a text can contain many linking words and still lack a sensible argument.
foundation: Read two sentences together before judging their connection. A pronoun can carry forward an established participant: A courier arrived. She carried a sealed envelope. Repeating courier is not an error, but she is economical when its reference is clear. This and that can also refer to a whole previous event: The envelope was empty. This caused concern. A summary noun, such as this omission, can identify the intended aspect more precisely. It is useful when several earlier facts could compete, not compulsory after every this.
intermediate: Build a reference chain by tracking a participant through noun phrases, pronouns and descriptions. A visitor, the visitor and she can form a chain. Do not vary technical labels just to avoid repeating a word: a permit, a licence and an authorisation may refer to different legal objects. Substitution replaces repeated material with a smaller expression: The red folder is damaged; use the blue one. Ellipsis leaves recoverable material unspoken: Mara can attend, but I cannot. The omitted content is attend, understood from the first clause.
advanced: Omission has grammatical and interpretative limits. In The first room was warm; the second, cold, the missing was is recoverable in a coordinated comparison. In a detached formal sentence such as The second cold, it may instead look like a fragment. So can substitute for a proposition after suitable verbs: I think so. Do so commonly substitutes for an action: The clerk promised to check and did so. It is not interchangeable with it or one in every context. Choose the substitute by the size and kind of unit being replaced.
expert: Reference can point backwards, forwards or outside the text. The first is often called anaphora, the second cataphora and the third deixis. A pronoun need not replace a single noun: propositional this can refer to a preceding clause or stretch of discourse. However, an editor should test whether readers recover the intended content rather than merely any plausible content. Cohesion also includes lexical repetition and relations such as part–whole. These support interpretation but do not establish truth or logical consequence. A therefore between unrelated claims creates a misleading inference rather than coherence.

patterns.meaning: Maintains a participant when reference is identifiable.
Avoids repeating material recoverable from context.

examples.sentence: A lamp failed. It was replaced immediately.
The first proposal was costly; the second, affordable.
examples.analysis: Was is recoverable in the second coordinated unit.

examples.sentence: The supplier promised to replace the faulty part and did so.
examples.analysis: Did so substitutes for replacing the part, not for the supplier.

contrasts.a: The archive closed early. This disrupted the visit.
contrasts.b: The archive closed early. This closure disrupted the visit.
contrasts.note: Both grammatical; the summary noun makes the event reference explicit.

exceptions: Informal situational ellipsis such as Ready? is normal conversation, though a formal standalone report usually supplies the full clause.

mistakes.problem: The clerk promised to inspect the meter and did one.
mistakes.repair: The clerk promised to inspect the meter and did so.
mistakes.reason: One substitutes for a suitable noun, not the inspection action.

mistakes.problem: A researcher challenged a manager after she altered the figures.
mistakes.repair: After the manager altered the figures, a researcher challenged her.
mistakes.reason: If the manager altered them, repeating the role removes the competing she reference.

glossary.definition: Linked expressions identifying a participant or topic.
Omission whose grammatical content is recoverable.

modules.title: Time, topics and the movement of information
modules.definition: Textual progression is the way a passage moves from established information to a developing point. Temporal consistency preserves intended time relationships, rather than requiring every verb to have one tense.
foundation: A reader needs to know how the next sentence relates to the current one. A useful default is to begin from something already identifiable and then develop it: The school opened a workshop. The workshop offers evening classes. You can also repeat a subject deliberately to maintain a topic. Beginning with new information is legitimate when introducing a contrast or changing focus. The practical question is whether the sequence guides the intended reader, not whether every sentence follows one fixed template or starts with a different word.
intermediate: Transitions express relations such as addition, contrast, concession, consequence and example. They do not create those relations. The route was shorter; nevertheless, it took longer expresses an unexpected contrast. The route was shorter; therefore, it took longer would require extra circumstances to explain the result. Topic sentences often state a paragraph’s controlling idea, but can occur after an opening example or be implicit. A paragraph may contain several related claims serving one purpose. Organise supporting details so that the relationship among them remains visible.
advanced: Tense choices can change purposefully within a paragraph. The clinic opened in 2018 and now treats patients daily contrasts a completed opening with an ongoing practice. A research summary may use the past for methods and the present for a still-relevant interpretation. A past perfect can place an event before the narrative reference point, after which ordinary past forms may continue the sequence. Voice also changes legitimately to maintain the topic: We received a damaged instrument. It was repaired the next day. The passive keeps the instrument in view.
expert: Theme and rheme are terms used in some linguistic frameworks for the point of departure of a clause and its development. Given and new describe information status, while topic and focus describe what is discussed and what is foregrounded. These distinctions overlap but are not identical. A passive, cleft or fronted phrase can organise information without altering the underlying event. Changes can nevertheless affect implication, contrast or presupposition. When revising an extended passage, compare its entire information route; a locally concise active sentence may break the established chain that a passive sentence maintained more effectively.

patterns.meaning: Separates a completed event from a current state.
Signals an outcome contrary to an expectation.

examples.sentence: The roof leaked last winter. It is secure now.
examples.analysis: A justified past-to-present shift distinguishes then from now.

examples.sentence: An old map was discovered. The map revealed a forgotten path.
examples.analysis: New map information becomes the next sentence’s topic.

examples.sentence: The laboratory rejected the first sample. A second sample was then requested.
examples.analysis: The voice changes, but the sequence remains coherent.

contrasts.a: The trial ended in May. The team now analyses the results.
contrasts.b: The trial ended in May. The team analysed the results.
contrasts.note: Both grammatical; the first describes current work, the second past work.

exceptions: A repeated opening can create clear thematic continuity; variation is a rhetorical choice, not a requirement to avoid the same subject three times.

mistakes.problem: The bridge opened yesterday and carries traffic last year.
mistakes.repair: The bridge opened yesterday and carries traffic now.
mistakes.reason: The supplied times cannot describe an already functioning bridge last year if it first opened yesterday.

mistakes.problem: The battery was empty. Therefore, the screen was brighter because of the empty battery.
mistakes.repair: The battery was empty. The screen was brighter.
mistakes.reason: Retain both stated observations while removing the unsupported causal assertion. The cause needs separate evidence; do not invent a different brightness event.

glossary.definition: Keeping a participant or issue traceable across sentences.
Material assumed identifiable to the reader in context.
glossary.example: the workshop in the second sentence

modules.title: Academic compression, hedging and economical variety
modules.definition: Grammatical compression expresses information with less explicit clausal structure; hedging adjusts commitment, scope or politeness. Neither compression nor formal vocabulary automatically improves a claim.
foundation: A verb can describe an event directly: The council approved the plan. A noun can package it for later discussion: This approval was unexpected. That change is nominalisation. It is useful when an earlier action becomes a new topic, or when a technical field needs an established concept. It can also conceal agents: approval of the plan leaves the approver unnamed. Ask which form gives readers the information they need. There is no universal rule that nouns are weak and verbs are strong.
intermediate: Compress only material whose contribution you understand. Because the samples were contaminated, the team repeated the test can become Because of sample contamination, the team repeated the test. The noun phrase is shorter, but it no longer states the contamination as a finite clause. A reduced relative can save words: the files that were damaged becomes the damaged files, though position and scope may change. Dense noun strings can obscure relations: student travel safety review may need a phrase explaining whose travel and what is being reviewed.
advanced: A cautious academic claim can mark uncertainty (may explain), evidential limits (the interviews suggest), frequency (often) or scope (in the sampled schools). These are different contributions. Removing one can exaggerate the evidence. A narrow claim is not necessarily well-supported; it still needs evidence. Likewise, a figure supplies precision but is not automatically a hedge. Several qualifications can be necessary if they perform distinct jobs: The small sample suggests that the change may help some learners. Avoid stacking synonyms that add no further distinction.
expert: Syntactic variety serves clarity when each structure fits its information task. Active clauses can identify actors; passives can maintain a topic or appropriately background an unknown actor; nominalisations can organise an argument; explicit clauses can unpack compressed relations. Register belongs to a genre and audience rather than a hierarchy of longer words. A first-person statement of method can be appropriate in academic prose if the discipline permits it. An editor should distinguish grammatical defects, unsupported assertions and optional stylistic changes, then preserve modality, attribution and logical relationships while improving the text.

patterns.meaning: Packages an event for further discussion.
Separates evidential support from modal possibility.

examples.sentence: The panel rejected the bid. This rejection delayed the project.
examples.analysis: The noun packages the earlier action as a topic.

examples.sentence: The interviews suggest that the policy may help new entrants.
examples.analysis: Suggest and may mark distinct aspects of commitment.

examples.sentence: Because the labels were missing, the samples could not be identified.
examples.analysis: An explicit causal clause can be clearer than a dense noun string.

contrasts.b: In this small trial, the treatment appeared to improve sleep.
contrasts.note: The second limits evidence and commitment; it is not interchangeable with the stronger claim.

exceptions: Purposeful repetition and a well-chosen passive may improve a text even when a shorter active alternative exists.

mistakes.problem: The survey proves all workers prefer remote work; only twelve volunteers responded.
mistakes.repair: The twelve volunteers’ responses suggest a preference for remote work within that small group.
mistakes.reason: The original exceeds the supplied evidence in certainty and population scope.

mistakes.problem: Due to the fact that the board made a decision to postpone the hearing, it was delayed.
mistakes.repair: Because the board decided to postpone the hearing, it was delayed.
mistakes.reason: The revision reduces avoidable wording while retaining the decision and consequence.

glossary.definition: Expressing an event, property or relation as a noun.
An expression adjusting commitment, scope or directness.

questions.prompt: What does it refer to in A parcel arrived. It was empty?
questions.why: It continues the established parcel noun phrase.

questions.prompt: Choose the meaningful substitute: She promised to inspect the valve and ____.
questions.why: Did so substitutes for the inspection action; one would substitute for a noun.

questions.prompt: Identify the genuine error: The ferry arrived yesterday. It carries passengers daily.
questions.why: The past arrival event and present habitual service justify different tenses.

questions.prompt: Which relation does nevertheless normally signal?
questions.why: Nevertheless presents a contrasting outcome that holds despite an expectation.

questions.prompt: All six interviewees expressed support. These interviews are the only evidence supplied. Which statement is appropriately limited to that evidence?
questions.why: The answer reports the observed group; the other claims extend beyond the supplied evidence.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of nominalisation?
questions.why: Approval packages the event as a noun; the other options use verb approve.

questions.prompt: After The report and the map were missing, which continuation explicitly identifies the map?
questions.why: Repeating map removes competition between two singular referents.

questions.prompt: Which is true of cohesion and coherence?
options: Coherence requires the same tense everywhere.
Every this must precede a noun.
A connector guarantees a valid argument.
Cohesive links can exist in an incoherent argument.
questions.why: Visible links do not establish logical sense or truth; tense and reference remain contextual.

questions.prompt: Which sentence explicitly retains possibility?
options: The measure certainly caused the change.
The measure must have caused the change.
The measure may have caused the change.
questions.why: May have caused expresses possibility rather than certainty or a strong deduction.

questions.prompt: Choose the genuine error in this formal passage: The first lease expired; the second did not.
questions.why: The omitted expire is recoverable after did not; the passage is grammatical.

questions.prompt: Trace reference in A technician entered. The technician checked a meter. She photographed it.
questions.model: Technician/the technician/she form one chain; a meter/it form another.
alternatives: Equivalent chain notation is valid.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference: The lift stopped. This worried us. / This breakdown worried us.
questions.model: Both are grammatical; breakdown specifies which aspect of the event caused worry.
alternatives: Other accurate explanations of specificity are valid.

questions.prompt: Complete with a substitute for a noun: The green pen is dry; try the black ____.
alternatives: The black pen repeats the noun and is also grammatical.

questions.prompt: Expand the omitted material: Sara can stay, but Imran cannot.
questions.model: Sara can stay, but Imran cannot stay.
alternatives: Cannot remain is a paraphrase rather than literal expansion.

questions.prompt: Order these sentences coherently: A This repair restored the supply. B A storm damaged the cable. C Engineers repaired it.
alternatives: Explain any other sequence that supplies an explicit prior context.

questions.prompt: Join with a suitable concession: The route was shorter. The journey took longer because traffic was heavy.
questions.model: The route was shorter; nevertheless, heavy traffic made the journey longer.
alternatives: Although the route was shorter, heavy traffic made the journey longer is valid.

questions.prompt: Explain why these tenses can coexist: The library opened in 2020 and now serves three villages.
questions.model: Opened locates the founding in a completed past; serves describes current operation.
alternatives: Equivalent clear explanation is valid.

questions.prompt: Package the first action as a noun: The committee postponed the vote. That action upset the delegates.
questions.model: The committee postponed the vote. This postponement upset the delegates.
alternatives: The postponement upset the delegates is also valid.

questions.prompt: Contrast The evidence proves the cause with The evidence suggests a possible cause.
questions.model: The first claims conclusive support; the second offers a tentative explanation.
rubric: Do not equate precision with certainty.
alternatives: Equivalent paraphrases are valid.

questions.prompt: The intended referent is the permit: The officer placed the permit beside the receipt. It was unsigned. Revise explicitly.
questions.model: The officer placed the permit beside the receipt. The permit was unsigned.
alternatives: The unsigned permit was placed beside the receipt by the officer is valid.

questions.prompt: Split while preserving cause: Because the sensor failed, the alarm did not sound.
questions.model: The sensor failed. As a result, the alarm did not sound.
alternatives: The alarm did not sound because of a sensor failure can be part of another valid split.

questions.prompt: Classify may, in the sampled towns and according to the survey as uncertainty, scope or attribution.
questions.model: May: uncertainty; in the sampled towns: scope; according to the survey: attribution.
alternatives: Context may give may permission, but the intended academic claim uses possibility.

questions.prompt: Why can replacing repeated legal term licence with permit cause a problem?
questions.model: The labels may have different legal meanings; varied wording can break reference or change the claim.
rubric: Do not assume synonyms are interchangeable.
alternatives: A context explicitly defining them as equivalent can permit variation.

questions.prompt: Edit without adding facts: A tank leaked yesterday. The caretaker repairs it then. This leakage has stopped now.
questions.model: A tank leaked yesterday. The caretaker repaired it then. The leak has stopped now.
alternatives: The caretaker repaired the tank yesterday is also possible.

questions.prompt: Is a passive always less cohesive? Evaluate: We received a damaged telescope. It was repaired immediately.
questions.model: No. The passive keeps the telescope as topic; We repaired it immediately is also coherent if we were the repairers.
alternatives: A different active repairer can be named only if known.

questions.prompt: The interviews ended last month. Complete: The interviewees ____ that transport was difficult, but this small sample ____ not establish a national pattern.
rubric: Past reporting for the supplied interviews.
alternatives: Said can replace reported. Could can fill the second gap; cannot establish is a possible full-clause rewrite only if the printed not is removed.

questions.prompt: Write two sentences cautiously describing a fictional trial in eight schools; do not generalise to every school.
questions.model: In a trial involving eight schools, attendance improved after the timetable changed. The small trial suggests a possible benefit, but it does not establish that the change caused the improvement.
alternatives: Original claims with the same limits are valid.

questions.prompt: Explain why therefore is unjustified here without more evidence: The office painted its door. Therefore, the river flooded.
questions.model: The connector claims a consequence, but no causal relation between painting and flooding has been supplied.
alternatives: A fictional context establishing an unusual mechanism could change the interpretation.

corrections.prompt: Correct for the stated past event: The inspection happened last Monday. The engineer checks the wiring during it.
corrections.model: The inspection happened last Monday. The engineer checked the wiring during it.
alternatives: Narrative present is possible only if explicitly adopted consistently.

corrections.prompt: No change if grammatical: The first applicant could attend; the second could not.
alternatives: Could not attend is a valid full version.

corrections.prompt: Correct: The report recommends a review. This recommendations was ignored.
corrections.model: The report recommends a review. This recommendation was ignored.
rubric: Make singular this agree with recommendation.
Retain ignored as the later event.
alternatives: These recommendations were ignored requires a genuinely plural source.

corrections.prompt: Clarify that the parcel, not the cupboard, was damaged: The parcel was in the cupboard. It was damaged.
corrections.model: The parcel was in the cupboard. The parcel was damaged.
alternatives: The damaged parcel was in the cupboard is valid.

corrections.prompt: Correct the unsupported universal: All residents support the project. The only evidence is a poll in which all five volunteer respondents supported it.
corrections.model: The five volunteers polled supported the project.
alternatives: The poll found support among its five volunteers is valid.

corrections.prompt: No change if grammatical: The machine failed in May. It is working now.
rubric: Retain both past failure and current operation.
alternatives: The machine, which failed in May, is working now is valid.

corrections.prompt: Repair the substitution: They promised to replace the faulty bulbs and did it so.
corrections.model: They promised to replace the faulty bulbs and did so.
rubric: Use did so for the action.
alternatives: They promised to replace the faulty bulbs, and they replaced them. The alternative must preserve both the promise and the completed replacement.

corrections.prompt: Edit for economy without strengthening the claim: It may possibly perhaps be the case that costs could rise.
rubric: Remove overlapping hedges that add no distinct scope here.
alternatives: Costs could rise is also valid.

transformations.prompt: Make the known samples the topic without inventing who tested them: Someone tested the samples twice.
rubric: Do not name an unknown tester.
alternatives: The samples underwent two tests is a possible paraphrase.

transformations.prompt: Replace the event clause with a nominalisation: Because the supplier withdrew, the project stopped.
transformations.model: Because of the supplier’s withdrawal, the project stopped.
alternatives: The supplier’s withdrawal stopped the project is valid if the causative meaning is intended.

writing.prompt: Write a 120–160-word fictional research update about a small transport survey. Include a clear reference chain, one justified tense shift, a transition, a useful nominalisation and a cautious conclusion.
writing.model:
In July, the team reported on a survey completed during the previous month. Twelve volunteer commuters had described irregular departures and crowded buses on their usual routes. These volunteers supplied useful accounts of their own journeys, but their responses do not represent every traveller. The survey ended in June; the team now compares the responses with published schedules. This comparison may reveal whether the reported late departures are concentrated at particular times. It will not, by itself, establish why delays occur or show that every route has the same problem. Further observations are therefore planned before recommendations are finalised. The team will record the time and location of each observation so that later readers can assess how far the findings apply. No national conclusion is justified by this small fictional exercise.

Analysis: These volunteers/their forms a reference chain. Ended…now compares is a justified time shift. Comparison is a useful nominalisation; therefore signals the evidence-to-plan relation. May reveal and no national conclusion limit the claims.
rubric: Keep the sample and reference chains identifiable.
Use tense changes for explicit time relations.
Keep attribution, uncertainty and scope distinct.
Review original writing through these features, without claiming an automatic writing grade.
alternatives: Other original updates meeting the constraints are valid.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 23: Why can a passive help preserve an established topic?
recall.model: It can put an already mentioned affected participant in subject position.
rubric: Avoid saying passive is always preferable.
alternatives: Use a concrete pair of examples.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 17: Give one epistemic and one deontic interpretation of must.
recall.model: She must be home can be a deduction; visitors must sign in imposes an obligation.
alternatives: Other correct modal examples are valid.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 4: What can this refer to in The flight was cancelled. This upset us?
recall.model: The cancellation event or proposition, not merely the noun flight.
rubric: Do not require an accompanying noun.
alternatives: An explicit summary noun can make the interpretation clearer.

checklist: I can identify each pronoun’s intended reference.
I can explain each tense shift.
I can distinguish evidence, uncertainty and scope.
I can preserve meaning while reducing wording.
